title: Opening; date and occasion
short: A grand commonplace on mortality opens a mock-heroic coronation in which the dying king of dullness, Flecknoe, crowns Thomas Shadwell as his heir.
body: The first couplet sounds like the start of a solemn state poem on mortality and royal succession, and the comedy lies in the gap between that register and its subject. Mac Flecknoe was probably written in 1676-77, when Shadwell was loudly claiming Ben Jonson as his model; it circulated in manuscript, was printed without authority in October 1682 (with a title page calling it a satire on the 'True-Blue-Protestant Poet, T.S.', a label from the Exclusion Crisis), and appeared in an authorised text in Miscellany Poems (1684). Older critics tied the poem to the political quarrel of 1682; manuscript evidence assembled by David Vieth and others points instead to a literary quarrel of the mid-1670s. It is the first great English mock-heroic and the model for Pope's Dunciad.

title: Flecknoe; like Augustus
short: Richard Flecknoe (d. c.1678), Irish-born Catholic priest and prolific minor poet, is the dying monarch of Nonsense, compared to the long-reigning Augustus.
body: Flecknoe published verse, letters and plays (Love's Kingdom, 1664, later serves as Shadwell's sceptre) and had already been mocked by Marvell in 'Flecknoe, an English Priest at Rome'. Like Augustus, who entered Roman politics at nineteen and ruled until AD 14, he came to power young and 'govern'd long'; Restoration panegyric habitually compared Charles II to Augustus, so the simile also mocks a courtly habit. Why Dryden chose Flecknoe as Shadwell's 'father' has never been fully explained (Hammond calls it a puzzle); he was a byword for copious bad writing, and his priesthood allows the jokes on unction and prophecy. The title uses the Gaelic patronymic 'Mac', making the Protestant Whig Shadwell son of an Irish Catholic priest.

anchor: Shadwell alone my perfect image bears
title: Shadwell
short: Thomas Shadwell (c.1640-1692), comic dramatist and self-proclaimed heir of Ben Jonson, Dryden's critical opponent and later his successor as Poet Laureate.
body: Shadwell wrote humours comedies such as The Sullen Lovers (1668), The Humorists (1671), Epsom Wells (1672) and The Virtuoso (1676), and an opera, Psyche (1675). In his prefaces he defended Jonson against Dryden's criticisms and hinted that Dryden's comedy was thin. Dryden's answer makes Shadwell the 'perfect image' of the dull Flecknoe, a parody of the Son as image of the Father (Hebrews 1:3). Lines 15-20 build the portrait through anaphora ('Shadwell alone') and climax in the famous paradox that he 'never deviates into sense'. After 1688 Shadwell replaced the Catholic Dryden as Laureate, an irony later readers often note.

title: lucid interval
short: A legal and medical term for a period of sanity in a madman; other dunces occasionally glimpse sense, Shadwell never.
body: In early modern law a 'lucid interval' was a temporary recovery of reason, during which a lunatic could, for instance, make a valid will (OED). Dryden turns the phrase into an image of light: beams of wit 'strike through' other minds, but Shadwell's 'genuine night' (genuine in its Latin sense of inborn) admits no ray, and his 'rising fogs' overcome the day. The imagery of fog and darkness returns at the coronation and in the 'damps of oblivion' that Flecknoe sheds. The following simile of 'monarch oaks' praises only Shadwell's bulk; 'supinely' means lying on the back, inertly.

title: types ... prepare thy way
short: Biblical typology: Heywood, Shirley and Flecknoe are forerunners of Shadwell as Old Testament figures and John the Baptist foreshadow Christ.
body: In Christian typology a 'type' is an earlier person or event that prefigures a later fulfilment. Dryden makes the prolific older dramatists Thomas Heywood and James Shirley 'types' of Shadwell, and casts Flecknoe as a John the Baptist 'sent before' to 'prepare thy way' (Matthew 3:3, quoting Isaiah 40:3). The Baptist wore camel's hair (Matthew 3:4); Flecknoe wears Norwich drugget, a coarse woollen cloth, which returns at the end as the mantle he leaves behind. 'Prophet of tautology' (needless repetition) mocks Shadwell's repetitive humours. The sacred parody is sustained to the final allusion to Elijah and Elisha.

title: the new Arion
short: Arion, the Greek singer saved by a dolphin charmed by his song; Shadwell, proud of his lute-playing, is pictured performing on the Thames.
body: Herodotus (1.23-24) tells how Arion, thrown overboard by sailors, was carried ashore by a dolphin. Flecknoe's own playing before King John IV of Portugal (whose patronage he boasted of) was only a 'prelude' to this triumph. The mock-epic diminishes everything: the 'trebles squeak', the echoes come from Pissing-Alley (a real London lane), the 'little fishes' throng to him as to the 'morning toast' floating on the river (toast was dipped in ale), and he beats time with his papers in a 'threshing hand'. The echo-device, in which places resound the hero's name, parodies pastoral and heroic convention; the line about 'Epsom blankets' glances at a blanket-tossing farce in Shadwell's comedies (Lynch cites The Virtuoso; other editors point to Epsom Wells).

title: St Andre; Psyche; Singleton and Villerius
short: St Andre was the French dancing-master of Shadwell's opera Psyche (1675); John Singleton, a court musician, sang Villerius in Davenant's Siege of Rhodes.
body: The pun on 'feet' joins dance steps with metrical feet: the verse of Psyche keeps time like a dancing master and its rhythm is as monotonous as tautology. Psyche, adapted from Moliere with music by Matthew Locke, was one of the costliest spectacles of the Restoration stage and was much ridiculed; Dryden returns to it repeatedly. So jealous is Singleton that he renounces 'the lute and sword' and vows never to play Villerius again, the Grand Master in Sir William Davenant's The Siege of Rhodes (1656), the first English opera. The point is that Jonson's would-be heir sought fame through music and spectacle rather than wit.

title: fair Augusta much to fears inclined
short: Augusta is London; its 'fears' are usually glossed as the panic of the Popish Plot (1678), which raises a problem for dating the poem.
body: Augusta was a Roman name for London. Many editors, Lynch among them, gloss the city's fears as the hysteria of the Popish Plot, the invented Jesuit conspiracy announced by Titus Oates in 1678. If the poem was written in 1676-77, as most scholars now think, the line either refers to earlier anxieties (plague, the Great Fire of 1666, recurrent fears of popery) or was added in revision before the 1682 printing. The parenthesis keeps the tone light: the 'fair' city is timorous, a hint at the credulity that Shadwell's Whig allies exploited.

title: Barbican; the mother-strumpets
short: The ruined Barbican watch-tower is now a district of brothels; the couplet parodies Cowley's Davideis, where the 'mother-waters' keep their court beneath the sea.
body: A barbican is an outer fortification guarding a gate; the old tower near Aldersgate had given its name to a poor quarter of brothels. Dryden describes it in mock-epic topography ('There stood of yore') and Spenserian diction ('hight', was called). In Book I of Abraham Cowley's Davideis (1656) the deep is a court where the mother-waters keep and sleep in silence; Dryden keeps the rhythm and nearly the words, substituting bawds for waters and the night-watch for the moon. Johnson noted that the Davideis had been imitated once, by Dryden in Mac Flecknoe. The pun on 'watch' (tower and constable) marks the decline from defence to vice.

title: Nursery; little Maximins
short: A training theatre for young actors near the Barbican, founded in the early 1660s, here the seminary of Shadwell's kingdom.
body: The Nursery was licensed in the early Restoration to train young actors for the patent companies; the RPO note dates it to 1662. Dryden's catalogue makes it a school for 'unfledged actors' and 'infant punks' (punk is slang for a prostitute), with the anaphora of 'Where' imitating epic descriptions of royal education. 'Little Maximins' refers to the blaspheming emperor Maximin in Dryden's own heroic play Tyrannic Love (1669), a sign that Dryden can laugh at his own bombast.

title: buskins ... socks; Simkin; clinches
short: The buskin (cothurnus) stands for tragedy and the sock (soccus) for comedy; neither Fletcher's tragedy nor Jonson's comedy is played at the Nursery.
body: Greek and Roman tragic actors wore the high boot (cothurnus, English buskin), comic actors the light shoe (soccus); Milton uses the pair in L'Allegro ('Jonson's learned sock') and Il Penseroso ('the buskin'd stage'). Dryden ranks 'Great Fletcher' and 'greater Jonson', the masters of the pre-war stage, above the Nursery's fare, which welcomes 'gentle Simkin', a clownish cobbler in drolls, and Panton, a noted punster. 'Clinches' are puns or quibbles (OED), which Restoration critics treated as the lowest form of wit.

title: ancient Decker; Misers, Raymond, Bruce
short: Thomas Dekker, who satirised Ben Jonson in Satiromastix (1601), becomes the prophet of Shadwell's reign, which will produce a catalogue of Shadwell's plays.
body: Dekker (c.1572-1632) sided against Jonson in the 'War of the Theatres', so it is apt that he foretells an anti-Jonsonian 'scourge of wit, and flail of sense'. The prophecy names Shadwell's works: Psyche (1675), The Miser (1672), The Humorists (1671) and The Hypocrite, with Raymond from The Humorists and Bruce from The Virtuoso. The genealogical catalogue parodies the prophecies of a hero's descendants in Virgil (Aeneid 6).

title: Martyrs of pies
short: Unsold books end as linings for pie-dishes and as lavatory paper; the sacred words 'martyrs' and 'reliques' make the waste comic.
body: Instead of Persian carpets, the coronation route is strewn with 'scatter'd limbs of mangled poets', torn sheets of unsold books. Waste paper was used by pastry cooks and in the privy, and the vocabulary of martyrdom and relics jokes on the Catholic colouring of the ceremony. Heywood, Shirley and John Ogilby (translator of Virgil and Homer) supply much of the litter, but Shadwell's works almost block the way. The 'bilk'd stationers' (booksellers cheated by unsaleable stock) form the guard under Henry Herringman, publisher of both Shadwell and Dryden. Pope reused the image in The Dunciad.

title: our young Ascanius ... Rome's other hope; lambent dulness; Hannibal
greek: Latin spes altera Romae; lambere 'to lick'
short: Shadwell is Ascanius, son of Aeneas; 'Rome's other hope' translates Virgil's spes altera Romae (Aeneid 12.168).
body: In the Aeneid Ascanius (Iulus) is the heir in whom Rome's future rests, called in Book 12 the 'second hope of great Rome'. The next couplet parodies Aeneid 2.682-84, where a harmless flame plays around the boy's head as an omen of greatness: here 'lambent dulness' plays round Shadwell's face and fogs replace the halo. 'Lambent' (licking, playing lightly) is a Latinism and an oxymoron with dulness. Shadwell then swears eternal war on wit as the boy Hannibal swore at an altar to be Rome's enemy (Livy 21.1).

title: The coronation regalia; twelve owls
short: The ceremony parodies an English coronation: unction, orb and sceptre become ale, Flecknoe's play Love's Kingdom, and a crown of poppies, with owls as omen.
body: At a coronation the monarch is anointed and holds the orb in the left hand, the sceptre in the right. Flecknoe, 'king by office, and as priest by trade', anoints his son himself; in Shadwell's 'sinister' (left, and ill-omened) hand he places a mug of ale instead of the orb, and in the right his own Love's Kingdom (1664). Poppies are the flowers of sleep. The omen of twelve owls, birds of night and solemn stupidity, parodies Livy 1.7, where Romulus wins the kingship by seeing twelve vultures to Remus' six. Readers would have remembered Charles II's coronation of 1661.

title: from Ireland ... To far Barbadoes
short: Flecknoe's blessing parodies prophecies of endless empire (Virgil's imperium sine fine, Luke 1:33), but this empire runs over the remote edges of the English world.
body: Jupiter promises Rome an empire without end (Aeneid 1.279), and Gabriel says of Christ that 'of his kingdom there shall be no end' (Luke 1:33). 'Of his dominion may no end be known' echoes both. The boundaries, Ireland and Barbados, were places of exile, plantation and transportation; Ireland also prepares the jibe at Shadwell's 'Irish pen'. 'Beyond Love's kingdom' puns on Flecknoe's play, and the people's 'Amen' turns the blessing into mock liturgy. Flecknoe then 'repels the raging god' like the Sibyl in Aeneid 6, an inspired prophet of dullness.

title: gentle George; Dorimant, Loveit, Cully, Cockwood, Fopling
short: Sir George Etherege, whose comic characters show true wit even in their fools, set against Shadwell's dull humours; Sedley's help with Epsom Wells is also mocked.
body: Cully comes from Etherege's The Comical Revenge (1664), Lady Cockwood from She Would If She Could (1668), and Dorimant, Mrs Loveit and Sir Fopling Flutter from The Man of Mode (March 1676), a reference that helps date the poem. In Etherege even the fools display the author's wit; in Shadwell they only 'justify their author's want of sense'. Flecknoe also forbids any 'alien Sedley' to 'lard' (enrich, as a cook threads fat into lean meat) Shadwell's 'hungry Epsom prose': Sir Charles Sedley wrote a prologue for Epsom Wells (1672) and was rumoured to have improved it. The passage restates Dryden's side of the wit-versus-humours quarrel.

title: Sir Formal; northern dedications
short: Sir Formal Trifle is the windy orator of Shadwell's The Virtuoso; the 'northern dedications' are Shadwell's flattering addresses to the Duke of Newcastle.
body: In The Virtuoso (1676) Sir Formal Trifle is a pompous rhetorician who cannot stop talking. Flecknoe tells Shadwell he need not 'labour to be dull': if he simply writes his best, Sir Formal's style will come unsought. The 'northern dedications' are Shadwell's dedications to William Cavendish, Duke of Newcastle, whose seat was in Nottinghamshire and who was himself a playwright and patron. The Virtuoso supplies the trap-door trick on which the poem ends.

title: Jonson's hostile name
short: The heart of the quarrel: Shadwell claimed to be Jonson's heir, and Flecknoe insists Jonson is no relation of theirs.
body: In prefaces to The Sullen Lovers, The Humorists and The Virtuoso, Shadwell praised Jonson's comedy of humours and defended it against Dryden. Here Flecknoe calls Jonson's name 'hostile' to their dynasty: 'Thou art my blood, where Jonson has no part.' The rhetorical questions that follow list Shadwell's faults (railing at learning, writing love in Prince Nicander's vein, promising a play and producing a farce, plagiarising Etherege) and ask where Jonson ever did any such thing. The proof by negation lets Dryden praise Jonson while degrading his self-appointed heir. Shadwell's lumbering wit is, like oil under water, always below Etherege's.

title: prince Nicander; whip-stitch
short: Nicander is a lover in Shadwell's Psyche; 'whip-stitch' and the vulgar tag after it are cant catch-phrases of Shadwell's comic characters.
body: Psyche (1675) gives Prince Nicander extravagant love-speeches, and 'swept the dust in Psyche's humble strain' mocks the opera's lowlier verse; Dryden asks whether Jonson ever wrote like that. To 'sell bargains' was to answer an innocent question with a coarse retort, a low form of repartee; 'whip-stitch' (in a moment) and 'kiss my a--e' are cant catch-phrases of Shadwell's comic characters, which editors trace to The Virtuoso. The dashes are the printer's own censorship, kept in this text.

title: bias
short: A figure from the game of bowls: the bias is the weight that makes a bowl curve; Shadwell's mind always curves towards dulness.
body: Shadwell prided himself on inventing new 'humours', after Jonson's theory that a character is governed by a ruling inclination. Dryden turns the idea against him: his one humour is a bias, the weight set into one side of a wooden bowl so that it runs in a curve (OED). His writings therefore 'lean on one side still', and whatever he attempts bends the same way. The conceit is sustained across six lines, a fine example of argument carried by the heroic couplet.

title: tympany; tun; kilderkin
short: A tympany is a swelling of the belly with wind; a tun is a great cask, a kilderkin a small one. Shadwell's bulk is air, not substance.
body: Flecknoe denies that Shadwell's 'mountain-belly' is a true likeness of his own: it is a 'tympany of sense', a morbid swelling, especially of the abdomen, caused by wind (OED). The cask images play on Shadwell's girth and drinking: a tun held about 252 gallons, a kilderkin, half a barrel, only 16 or 18. The antithesis 'tun of man' / 'kilderkin of wit' is a showpiece of Dryden's balanced couplet.

title: Irish pen
short: Folklore held that no venomous creature could live in Ireland; the venom in Shadwell's heart dies the moment it touches his 'Irish' pen.
body: According to legend St Patrick drove the snakes from Ireland, and it was said that nothing venomous could survive there. The jibe also extends the fiction of Shadwell's descent from the Irish priest Flecknoe, an insult to a vehemently Protestant Whig. His satires are 'inoffensive' and 'never bite', unlike Dryden's own. Flecknoe concludes that his son's genius lies not in 'keen Iambics' (satire, after the Greek iambic lampoon) but in harmless verbal toys.

title: Acrostic land; wings and altars
short: Shadwell is sent to the minor genres of anagram, acrostic and shaped verse, poems printed in the form of wings or altars.
body: An acrostic spells a word with the initial letters of its lines; a pattern poem is laid out on the page in a shape, like George Herbert's 'Easter Wings' and 'The Altar' (1633), a fashion of the early seventeenth century. By the Restoration such verbal games were regarded as false wit, the 'torture' of one word 'ten thousand ways', a judgement Addison later developed in Spectator 58-63. Flecknoe's last advice, to set and sing his own songs to the lute, brings the poem back to Shadwell's music.

title: The trap-door; the mantle and double portion
short: Flecknoe falls through a trap-door borrowed from The Virtuoso; his mantle passes to Shadwell as Elijah's to Elisha, with a 'double portion' of dulness (2 Kings 2).
body: In The Virtuoso the wits Bruce and Longvil drop the orator Sir Formal through a trap-door in mid-speech; Shadwell's own stage trick now silences the 'yet declaiming' Flecknoe. In 2 Kings 2:9-13 Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah's spirit, Elijah is taken up in a whirlwind, and his mantle falls to his successor. Dryden inverts the miracle: the prophet goes down, while his drugget robe rises on a flatulent 'subterranean wind', and the young prophet inherits twice his father's 'art'. The couplet completes the frame of succession and the biblical parody that began with the forerunner and the 'types'.
